methods.title: Focused compound library and direction of receptor modulation
paragraphs: A focused library of 16 chemically defined parent compounds compared receptor-engagement patterns relevant to the PDGFRA/FLT4 priorities. Nintedanib served as the index drug; imatinib, crenolanib, avapritinib and ripretinib provided PDGFRA-directed comparator chemistry; axitinib, tivozanib, lenvatinib, sunitinib, pazopanib, sorafenib, regorafenib and ponatinib represented VEGFR or multikinase inhibitors; MAZ51 was a nonclinical FLT4 probe. Pirfenidone and nerandomilast supplied clinically relevant nonkinase comparators, without assuming that either was a verified nonbinder. Parent identity, stereochemistry, source accessions, regulatory indications and hepatic warnings were recorded for every compound. Nintedanib retained the Z keto-enamine parent, MAZ51 the Z isomer, and nerandomilast the label-consistent R sulfoxide. Comparisons addressed differential engagement rather than presuming that stronger dual inhibition would improve hepatic safety: PDGFRA deletion has context-dependent effects in liver injury, whereas VEGFR3 inhibition can impair lymphatic repair [105, 106].

Published ChEMBL activities were evaluated separately by endpoint, assay context, species annotation, variant description, validity and duplicate status. The complete disposition retained all 191 retrieved activity records. The exact-value summary required human target mapping, no described variant, a linked source document and no validity or duplicate flag; identified secondary-source reviews were excluded; unspecified constructs were not relabelled as experimentally verified wild type. Kd, Ki and IC50 were kept separate, and censored values retained their inequalities. A source-matched Davis kinase-binding panel provided a descriptive biochemical comparison [54]; records flagged as repetitions of earlier measurements were identified and were not counted as independent observations [107]. An internal PDGFRA/PDGFRB Kd inconsistency in the crenolanib primary report prevented selection of a single definitive value for calibration. The full library and all record-level decisions are provided in Additional file 8.

methods.title: AI-assisted protein–ligand screening and molecular properties
paragraphs: Each compound was submitted against canonical PDGFRA residues 593–954 or FLT4 residues 845–1173 through the Boltz small-molecule library-screen service on 2 October 2026 [108]. The recorded engine and pipeline were boltzmol version 1.0, accessed with boltz-api 0.43.0. Exact parent SMILES and a single protein chain were supplied, with nintedanib as the reference ligand for pocket localization. Provider-default structural-alert filters were retained. Every submitted compound received a final disposition; filtered compounds were recorded as unscored rather than assigned zero affinity. Scored compounds were ordered by the returned binding_confidence within each target. Optimization score, structural confidence, interface metrics and predicted Tier-1 solubility, permeability and logD were retained separately. These dimensionless model outputs were not converted into Kd or compared as calibrated cross-target selectivity. Input sequences, structures, metadata and raw result files are supplied in Additional file 9.

Inductive Bio predicted logD at pH 7.4 and the most acidic and basic pKa for the same 16 structures [109]. The respective model versions were 1.7.0, 1.4.0 and 1.4.0; the existing nintedanib predictions used identical model and configuration versions and were retained. Returned canonical SMILES were checked against the submitted stereospecific InChIKeys. Model bounds, out-of-domain flags and low-confidence flags were preserved. Differences from nintedanib were descriptive within-model contrasts. The provider did not specify coverage for its returned bounds, which were therefore not labelled confidence intervals. These predictions characterized molecular properties rather than hepatic exposure or clinical safety.

methods.title: Structure-based docking and receptor-conformation sensitivity
paragraphs: Independent rigid-receptor docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, Meeko 0.8.0 and RDKit 2026.03.6 [98–100]. The PDGFRA receptor was the wild-type imatinib complex 6JOL at 1.90 Å resolution; all coordinate-bearing residues matched the canonical sequence [104]. The primary grid encompassed the deposited imatinib heavy atoms with a 6 Å margin on each face and a minimum dimension of 22 Å. Imatinib was independently embedded and redocked as a crystallographic control; symmetry-aware ligand heavy-atom RMSD was measured without fitting the ligand to its crystal coordinates. For FLT4, the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database model AF-P35916-F1 version 6, retrieved through Proto, was cropped to residues 845–1173 [101–103]. Version 6 denotes the database file version. The experimental VEGFR2–nintedanib complex 3C7Q defined the homologous pocket by sequence-guided structural alignment [26]; it was not treated as an experimental FLT4 complex. The alignment retained 222 core Cα pairs with RMSD 1.074 Å, and the FLT4 pocket had mean pLDDT 85.88.

All 32 compound–target combinations underwent three independently initialized searches with fixed seeds 104729, 130363 and 155921, ETKDGv3 embedding, MMFF minimization and Vina exhaustiveness 32. Up to ten poses within 5 kcal/mol were retained per search. The three seeds measured computational search consistency and did not increase biological sample size. Median scores, observed ranges and pose consistency were reported descriptively. Supplied parent protonation/tautomer states were used without microspecies enumeration. Receptor conformation, predicted FLT4 coordinates and absent explicit solvent restrict interpretation of the scores. Protein–ligand contacts were defined as heavy-atom distances below 4 Å; proximity alone was not classified as a hydrogen bond. Full grid coordinates, receptor preparation, poses, logs and software versions are provided in Additional files 7–9.

results_title: Receptor-focused screening identifies complementary pharmacological comparators
results: The 16-compound comparison connected the receptor priorities to chemically and clinically interpretable perturbations. The experimental source-matched panel distinguished nintedanib binding to both receptors (PDGFRA/FLT4 Kd, 16/95 nM) from imatinib's PDGFRA-dominant profile (31/>10,000 nM); axitinib showed 0.51/170 nM [54, 107] (Fig. 7A). This separation supplied a mechanistic comparison across engagement patterns, while the full endpoint-specific activity record retained differences in assay context and construct annotation (Additional file 8).

BoltzMol returned scored pocket models for 12 compounds per target. Default structural-alert filtering excluded nintedanib, sunitinib, ponatinib and MAZ51 from both AI screens; this filtering supplied no evidence for or against their binding. Among scored compounds, PDGFRA binding-confidence values were highest for crenolanib (0.921), ripretinib (0.849) and axitinib (0.845). FLT4 values were highest for tivozanib (0.789), lenvatinib (0.754) and pazopanib (0.747) (Fig. 7B,C). Imatinib scored 0.804 for PDGFRA and 0.245 for FLT4, qualitatively consistent with its matched biochemical profile. Pirfenidone scored 0.232/0.139 and nerandomilast 0.027/0.035 for PDGFRA/FLT4, respectively. These predictions support their inclusion as nonkinase clinical comparators without establishing experimental nonbinding or hepatic superiority.

Crystallographic redocking reproduced the imatinib pose in PDGFRA with a symmetry-aware heavy-atom RMSD of 0.574 Å (Fig. 7D). The AI-exported imatinib–PDGFRA and tivozanib–FLT4 pocket models placed ligand atoms 2.930 and 2.975 Å from the backbone nitrogen of Cys677 and Cys930, respectively (Fig. 7E,F); these distances describe predicted proximity. The exported pocket structures contained 199 of 362 and 195 of 329 submitted receptor residues and therefore represented local binding models. Independent docking covered all 16 compounds, including those filtered from the AI screen. All primary seed-level scores and pose-consistency results, together with the separately reported receptor-conformation sensitivity, are retained in Supplementary Figures S13 and S14 and Additional files 7–9.

The property models returned all 48 requested Inductive predictions. Predicted logD at pH 7.4 ranged from 1.376 for pirfenidone to 4.604 for regorafenib, compared with 2.523 for nintedanib. Eight pKa predictions carried out-of-domain flags and three carried low-confidence flags; none of the logD predictions carried either flag (Supplementary Fig. S14; Additional file 8). Together, the biochemical, structural and property evidence identifies a complementary compound panel for exposure-controlled receptor perturbation. Its translational role is to test engagement-dependent injury and pulmonary responses, with the approved indication and hepatic warnings of each compound retained.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Liver injury can interrupt nintedanib treatment for fibrosing interstitial lung disease. We integrated human injury proteins, drug pharmacology and liver-cell networks to prioritize receptors and pharmacological comparators for mechanistic investigation.

Methods: Active-comparator pharmacovigilance, 13 human serum proteins, biochemical and cellular drug responses, and a five-donor liver atlas informed donor-balanced network integration. Six aggregation algorithms, matched-background calibration, donor omission and weight perturbation assessed candidate selection. Independent hepatic profiles from 22 mice and pulmonary datasets evaluated tissue context. A 16-compound library underwent AI-assisted screening, crystallographically controlled docking and molecular-property prediction.

Results: PDGFRA and FLT4 ranked first and second under four aggregation rules and remained among the top five in all 5000 weight perturbations. Reported dissociation constants were 16 and 95 nM, respectively. The narrow hepatic reporting odds ratio for nintedanib versus pirfenidone was 3.997 (95% confidence interval 3.226–4.951), with temporal heterogeneity. Competitive ranking and network interventions did not establish significant enrichment. Independent liver analysis identified decreased Kdr expression within the candidate family (q=0.0386; genome-wide q=0.119). AI screening scored 12 compounds per receptor, distinguishing imatinib's receptor profile and low-scoring nonkinase clinical comparators. PDGFRA imatinib redocking reproduced the crystal pose at 0.574 Å RMSD.

Conclusions: PDGFRA and FLT4 are reproducible priorities for investigating nintedanib-associated liver injury. Complementary pharmacological comparators enable exposure-controlled perturbation and rescue studies that measure hepatic injury while preserving pulmonary antifibrotic activity. The protective intervention direction remains to be established.
discussion: The compound comparison makes the target priorities experimentally actionable. Imatinib provides a PDGFRA-engaging comparator with weak FLT4 binding in a matched biochemical panel, while VEGFR-directed agents sample a different receptor profile. The nonkinase pulmonary treatments pirfenidone and nerandomilast broaden the comparison to clinically relevant pharmacology. Together, these compounds can distinguish receptor dependence from a response shared by structurally unrelated drugs. The clinical objective remains an exposure-matched reduction in injury with preserved pulmonary activity; approved oncology use or a favorable computational score does not establish suitability for antifibrotic substitution.

The direction of intervention depends on the hepatic compartment. Conditional PDGFRA deletion in stellate cells has attenuated injury and fibrosis in some experimental settings, with different effects across injury models [105]. In contrast, VEGFR3 inhibition impaired lymphangiogenesis, drainage and reparative responses after hepatic ischemia–reperfusion [106]. This biology favors testing selective receptor perturbations and reciprocal rescue before advancing systemic dual inhibition. A FLT4-sparing engagement pattern is therefore a mechanistic hypothesis to evaluate alongside retained pulmonary activity, not an established explanation for nintedanib-associated injury.
